description:
pkix-chain/src/aia_extract.rs:77-90 implements case-insensitive scheme prefix matching with a hand-rolled closure:

```rust
let lower_prefix = |p: &str| {
    uri.len() > p.len()
        && uri.as_bytes()[..p.len()]
            .iter()
            .map(|b| b.to_ascii_lowercase())
            .eq(p.bytes())
};
lower_prefix("http://") || lower_prefix("https://")
```

The standard library has had `[u8]::eq_ignore_ascii_case` stable since Rust 1.23 (2018). The equivalent idiomatic form is:

```rust
let bytes = uri.as_bytes();
(bytes.len() > 7 && bytes[..7].eq_ignore_ascii_case(b"http://"))
    || (bytes.len() > 8 && bytes[..8].eq_ignore_ascii_case(b"https://"))
```

Or, using `str::get` to avoid the manual length gate:

```rust
uri.get(..7).is_some_and(|s| s.eq_ignore_ascii_case("http://")) && uri.len() > 7
```

(The `len > p.len()` gate is load-bearing — the existing tests at lines 110-113 enforce that `"http:"` and `"http:/x"` are rejected, so a literal-equal check is not sufficient.)

What goes wrong if it stays: every reader has to mentally execute the byte-by-byte iterator pipeline to confirm the closure does what its name says. The standard-library helper is the one-line, well-known primitive for this exact operation. A serious Rust reviewer reading this code would ask "why did you not use `eq_ignore_ascii_case`?" — and there is no good answer.
title: is_http_scheme reinvents <[u8]>::eq_ignore_ascii_case via hand-rolled closure
